evals.prompt: I'm using pptxgenjs to build a slide with a bright red rounded-rectangle shape, and I want it to cast a shadow that appears to come from below the shape (i.e., the shadow is cast upward, above the shape) rather than the usual downward-and-right shadow. What color value should I pass for the red fill, and what shadow angle and offset should I use to achieve the upward cast without corrupting the .pptx file?
evals.expected_output: The two choices here are both explicit corruption landmines in the 'Creating with pptxgenjs — gotchas' section. For the fill, SKILL.md says: "Hex colors: never #, never 8 digits. color: "FF0000". Both "#FF0000" and alpha baked into the hex ("00000020") corrupt the file." So the agent should pass color: "FF0000" — six hex digits, no leading #, and no alpha channel appended; using "#FF0000" or an 8-digit value like "00000020" would corrupt the file per that rule. For the shadow, SKILL.md says: "Shadow offset must be ≥ 0 — a negative offset corrupts the file. To cast a shadow upward, use angle: 270 with a positive offset." So to cast the shadow upward the agent must set angle: 270 together with a positive offset value (e.g. offset: 3) — never a negative offset, even though a naive reading of "upward" might suggest a negative offset is what's needed. Getting either of these two choices wrong (a #-prefixed or 8-digit hex color, or a negative shadow offset) independently corrupts the output file per these two named rules.
expectations: Uses color: "FF0000" for the fill — six hex digits, no leading #, no alpha channel appended.
Explicitly avoids "#FF0000" and any alpha-appended 8-digit hex (e.g. "00000020"), and states either would corrupt the file.
Sets the shadow's angle to 270 to achieve the upward cast, rather than assuming a negative offset does it.
Uses a positive offset value for the shadow, never a negative one.
States that a negative shadow offset corrupts the file, not merely that it looks wrong.

evals.prompt: I'm building a combo chart with pptxgenjs: a bar series plotted on the primary axis and a line series plotted on a secondary axis, using secondaryValAxis: true and secondaryCatAxis: true on the line series so it gets its own scale. Besides the two series definitions in the array passed to addChart(), what else do I need to configure in the chart options, and what happens if I forget it?
evals.expected_output: SKILL.md calls this out as a specific corruption trap in the pptxgenjs gotchas list: "A combo series using secondaryValAxis/secondaryCatAxis needs both valAxes and catAxes on the chart options, two entries each. Without them pptxgenjs writes axis ids it never declares, and PowerPoint discards that chart and reports the file as corrupt. Supplying only valAxes is not enough." So the agent must add both a valAxes array and a catAxes array to the chart's options object, each containing two entries (one for the primary axis, one for the secondary axis) — not just valAxes alone. If either array is omitted, or if only valAxes is supplied, pptxgenjs will reference axis ids in the chart XML that are never declared in the options; per the rule, PowerPoint will then discard the entire chart and report the file as corrupt. The fix belongs in the chart options object passed to addChart() itself, not as a post-processing step on the generated file.
expectations: States that the chart options object must include both valAxes and catAxes, not just valAxes.
States each of valAxes and catAxes must contain two entries (one primary, one secondary axis).
Explicitly states supplying only valAxes is not enough.
Explains the failure mode: without both, pptxgenjs writes axis ids it never declares, and PowerPoint discards the chart and reports the file as corrupt.
Ties this requirement specifically to the series using secondaryValAxis/secondaryCatAxis.

evals.prompt: I'm building a stacked column chart in pptxgenjs to show quarterly sales by region, and I want data labels on each segment positioned just outside the top of each stacked segment for legibility — i.e. dataLabelPosition: "outEnd". Is that a safe setting to use here, and what should I actually use?
evals.expected_output: SKILL.md's gotchas list has a rule specific to stacked charts: "On a stacked bar or column chart, dataLabelPosition must be ctr, inEnd, or inBase. outEnd corrupts the file." So outEnd is unsafe here — the correct answer identifies it as one of the file-corrupting values called out in the pptxgenjs section (alongside the negative-shadow-offset and hex-color traps) and instead recommends one of ctr, inEnd, or inBase. The agent should also flag that showValue: true is needed for labels to render at all, per the earlier default-charts rule ("Set showTitle + title, showValue: true + dataLabelPosition..."), but dataLabelPosition itself must be drawn from the three-value stacked-chart allowlist, never outEnd, regardless of the legibility argument for placing labels outside the bar.
expectations: Identifies dataLabelPosition: "outEnd" as unsafe for a stacked column chart and states it corrupts the file, not merely that it looks wrong.
Recommends dataLabelPosition be one of ctr, inEnd, or inBase.
Does not recommend or use outEnd anywhere in the final answer, despite the user's stated preference for outside-the-bar labels.
Notes showValue: true is also needed for the labels to render, per the default-charts rule.

evals.prompt: I'm writing a pptxgenjs script for a widescreen presentation. Without ever calling pres.layout, I add a slide and place a footer text box at x: 12.5, y: 7.0, assuming the canvas is the standard 13.3-inch-wide widescreen size. When I open the generated .pptx, will PowerPoint show an error, will the box get moved onto the visible slide, or something else? What should I change?
evals.expected_output: SKILL.md's first pptxgenjs gotcha covers exactly this: "Set pres.layout before adding slides. The default canvas is LAYOUT_16x9 = 10" × 5.625", not 13.3" wide. Coordinates past the edge are written, not clamped — the shape just isn't on the slide. (LAYOUT_WIDE is 13.3" × 7.5".)" Since the script never sets pres.layout, the default canvas is 10" × 5.625", not the assumed 13.3" × 7.5". Placing the footer at x: 12.5, y: 7.0 puts it well past both the width (10") and height (5.625") edges of that default canvas. Per the rule, pptxgenjs does not clamp those coordinates back onto the slide and does not raise an error — it writes them as-is, so the footer box is simply absent from the visible slide when opened in PowerPoint. The fix is to call pres.layout = "LAYOUT_WIDE" before adding any slides, which sets the 13.3" × 7.5" canvas the script's coordinates were actually written for.
expectations: States the default canvas without pres.layout set is LAYOUT_16x9 = 10" × 5.625", not 13.3" wide.
Identifies that x: 12.5, y: 7.0 falls outside that default canvas's edges.
States the shape will not raise an error and will not be clamped back onto the slide — it is written but simply doesn't appear on the slide.
Recommends setting pres.layout to LAYOUT_WIDE (13.3" × 7.5") to get the canvas the coordinates were written for.
States the layout must be set before slides are added, not after.

evals.prompt: Here's a draft design for a content card on a slide: a white rounded rectangle with a 0.15-inch-wide vertical stripe in the accent color running down its left edge, meant to visually separate the card from the rest of the slide and to serve as a repeating motif across the deck. Does this follow the design guidance in the skill, or should something change?
evals.expected_output: This stripe is explicitly called out in the Design Ideas 'Avoid (Common Mistakes)' list: "NEVER add decorative color bars or accent stripes — this includes: header/footer bars spanning the slide width, vertical sidebar stripes down one edge of the slide, thin accent stripes along one edge of a card or content block, and 'single-side borders' on rectangles. These read as AI-generated filler." A left-edge accent stripe on a content card matches "thin accent stripes along one edge of a card or content block" precisely, so it should be flagged and removed rather than kept as the deck's motif — the motif guidance earlier in the same section reinforces this directly: "Do not use a color bar or accent stripe as your motif (see Avoid list)." The rule then names the sanctioned alternatives: "If you want to set a card apart, use a subtle background tint, a drop shadow, or an icon — not an edge stripe." So the corrected design should replace the stripe with one of those three: a subtle background tint, a drop shadow, or an icon.
expectations: Flags the left-edge stripe as violating the 'NEVER add decorative color bars or accent stripes' rule.
Identifies it specifically as matching 'thin accent stripes along one edge of a card or content block.'
States the stripe should be removed rather than kept as the deck's repeating motif, referencing that a stripe must not be used as a motif.
Notes the rule characterizes such stripes as reading like AI-generated filler.
Suggests at least one of the three sanctioned alternatives: a subtle background tint, a drop shadow, or an icon.

evals.prompt: I just finished a deck built by editing a client-supplied PowerPoint template: I unzipped client-template.pptx, edited the slide XML directly, and re-zipped the result as out.pptx. All slide titles use Georgia per the client's brand guidelines. I converted the deck to images with soffice/pdftoppm and looked at every slide — none of the titles appear cut off. What QA steps do I still need to run before calling this done, and can I trust that the titles fit based on what I saw in those images?
evals.expected_output: The QA (Required) section lays out three passes in order — Content QA, File QA, Visual QA — and this deck triggers extra requirements in two of them. First, Content QA: run markitdown output.pptx to check for missing content, typos, and wrong order, and since this came from a template, also run the placeholder-leftover grep the skill specifies: "markitdown output.pptx | grep -iE \"\\bx{3,}\\b|lorem|ipsum|\\bTODO|\\[insert|this.*(page|slide).*layout\"" — "If grep returns results, fix them before declaring success." Second, File QA (required): because this deck came from a template, SKILL.md says "If the deck came from a template, always pass --original. A template may itself contain parts the XSD rejects, so a bare run can report failures you never caused — and a genuine regression can hide among them. --original baselines the schema and slide checks against the template, suppressing errors it already had." So the command must be python scripts/office/validate.py out.pptx --original client-template.pptx, not a bare run. Third, on the visual inspection already done: the Visual QA section says to check text overflow first, but adds a caveat that applies directly here — Georgia is named in Typography as one of the "QA-unreliable fonts (substitute has different widths — overflow checks can be wrong): Georgia, Trebuchet MS, Impact, Arial Black, Garamond, Consolas, Palatino Linotype," and the Visual QA section says explicitly: "(For a font the previewer renders unreliably per Typography, the preview is approximate: trust the ~10% slack you left, not its apparent fit.)" Since Georgia is on that list, the clean-looking title renders cannot be treated as proof the titles fit in real PowerPoint — the agent must instead confirm the title containers were sized with the ~10% extra slack Typography calls for when a non-safe-list font is used at the user's request, and should flag that the LibreOffice-rendered preview for those Georgia titles is only approximate.
expectations: Runs Content QA via markitdown output.pptx, including the placeholder-text grep (lorem/TODO/[insert/etc.) because the deck came from a template.
Runs File QA with validate.py ... --original client-template.pptx (or equivalent), explicitly including --original because the deck was built from a template.

Explains why --original is required for template-derived decks — it baselines schema/slide checks against the template so the template's own pre-existing issues aren't misattributed as new regressions.
Identifies Georgia as one of the 'QA-unreliable fonts' listed in the Typography section.
States that the clean-looking title renders cannot be trusted as proof of fit for Georgia — the agent must rely on the ~10% extra slack left in sizing rather than the preview's apparent fit.
